body.objective: Students will be able to develop a play idea.
body.iCan: I can develop a play idea.
successCriteria: I can generate a play idea from a character, a want and an obstacle
I can outline a one-act with a clear dramatic structure
I can write an opening scene with conflict
body.hook: Every play you've ever seen started as a blank page and one question: "What if...?" What if a girl buried her brother against the king's law? What if two men waited for someone who never came? Playwrights start small, with a character who wants something badly.

vocabulary.definition: The basic idea of a play in one or two sentences.
The struggle between opposing forces that drives the story.
The event that starts the main conflict.
The moment of highest tension, where the conflict is decided.
A short play performed without an intermission, usually 10 to 40 minutes.

study.title: What If?
study.question: How do playwrights turn a small idea into a dramatic structure?
study.passage:
Part 1, Idea generators (10 minutes): Try three: (a) a headline from local news; (b) a photo of a stranger: who are they, what do they want today?; (c) a "What if...?" question ("What if a teenager found out their grandfather was famous?").
Part 2, Premise (10 minutes): Choose one. Write: "[Character] wants [goal] but [obstacle], so [what they do]."
Part 3, Structure (15 minutes): Map your one-act using Freytag's pyramid: exposition (world and characters), inciting incident, rising action (three escalating complications), climax, falling action, resolution. Keep it to two or three characters and one location; one-acts work best tight.
Part 4, Opening page (15 minutes): Write the first page. Rules: start late (in the middle of something happening), show conflict within the first page, let dialogue reveal character, keep stage directions brief.
Script format: CHARACTER NAMES in capitals, dialogue below, (stage directions in parentheses and italics).
study.source: Original writing workshop for this lesson; structure based on Freytag's pyramid.
steps: Generate ideas from three starting points
Map the play on Freytag's pyramid
Write the first page in script format
Share a reading and get feedback
discussion: Which idea generator gave you the most surprising idea?
Why should a one-act have few characters and one location?
What does "start late" mean and why does it help?
Where in your outline does tension peak?
study.product: Submit a premise, a structure map and the first three pages of an original one-act play, then hold a table read with classmates.

examples.title: Premise
examples.problem: Write a premise about a missed flight.
examples.answer: A nervous student wants to reach her sister's wedding but misses the flight, so she must convince a grumpy stranger to drive her

examples.title: Inciting incident
examples.problem: What is the inciting incident in "Antigone"?
examples.answer: Creon forbids the burial of Polynices

examples.title: Start late
examples.problem: Improve an opening where two characters say hello and chat about weather.
examples.answer: Start with one character already packing to leave and the other blocking the door

examples.title: Script format
examples.problem: Format a line where Sam whispers "Don't."

practice.a: The basic idea of a play in one or two sentences.
A short play without an intermission.
Character wants goal but obstacle, so action.
The event that starts the main conflict.

practice.q: Name the stages of Freytag's pyramid.
practice.a: Exposition, inciting incident, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.

practice.q: Why limit characters in a one-act?
practice.a: It keeps the story focused and manageable.

practice.q: How are stage directions written in a script?
practice.a: In parentheses, often in italics, brief.
Begin in the middle of action rather than with set-up.

practice.q: Why must conflict escalate in rising action?
practice.a: Increasing stakes keep the audience engaged.
Word choice, rhythm and what characters avoid saying.

practice.q: Why should a playwright hear a table read?
practice.a: To hear what works aloud and find unclear or slow moments.

practice.q: What's the difference between a situation and a conflict?
practice.a: A situation is a setting; conflict needs a character wanting something against an obstacle.

misconceptions: Thinking a play needs many characters and locations
Starting with lots of polite small talk
Writing long stage directions instead of letting dialogue work
exitTicket: Write your premise using the formula.
Name the inciting incident in your play.
